overview: The LAAA Team of Marcus & Millichap is pleased to present 6617 Orange Street, a 21-unit apartment building in the Beverly Grove neighborhood of Los Angeles. Built in 1962, the building is three stories of wood frame served by a hydraulic elevator, 20,768 SF per the county on a 13,479 SF lot zoned R3-1-O, with an attached 12-car carport, a common laundry room and a resident manager. The mix is 15 one-bedroom, one-bath units and 6 two-bedroom, two-bath units, and 20 of the 21 units have balconies.

Ownership's rent roll as of September 2026 schedules $46,008 per month across 20 rent-paying units, with unit 201 occupied by the resident manager. One-bedroom rents run $2,050 to $2,495 and average $2,178; the five rent-paying two-bedrooms run $2,450 to $2,945 and average $2,669. Laundry adds about $350 per month.

The building has been under the same ownership since 1979, and the work a buyer usually has to price in is done: the soft-story retrofit (2018), the balcony repair (2024), the roof (2017) and the electrical subpanels (2023). All 21 units are under the Rent Stabilization Ordinance, so rent growth arrives as tenants move out on their own rather than by plan, and the building's own recent one-bedroom asking rent of $2,350 shows where a turned unit leases today.
properties.location_title: Beverly Grove, Walk Score 95, Rail Within a Half Mile
location_narrative: The property sits in Beverly Grove in the Wilshire community plan area and Council District 5, on a residential street of 1950s and 1960s apartment buildings. Measured in straight lines from the building, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center is 0.9 mile northwest, the Beverly Center 0.8 mile northwest, LACMA and the Miracle Mile museums 0.7 mile east, and The Grove and the Farmers Market 0.9 mile northeast. The city places the parcel within a half mile of a major transit stop; the nearest is the Metro D Line station at Wilshire and La Cienega.

The 90048 ZIP code reports a median household income of $103,495 and a median home value of $1,932,000, and 72% of its households rent. The parcel scores 95 on Walk Score, 65 on Transit Score and 71 on Bike Score, and sits outside the FEMA special flood hazard area.

This is a renter's location with demand on every side: hospital employment at Cedars-Sinai, retail at The Grove and the Beverly Center, and a rail station within walking distance. Buyers of rent-stabilized buildings pay for that depth because it keeps turned units leasing quickly at market.
physical_narrative: The certificate of occupancy issued September 20, 1962 describes a three-story Type V apartment building of 21 units with an attached 12-car carport and 21 required parking spaces. The county carries 20,768 SF of building area on a 13,479 SF interior lot. A hydraulic elevator serves the floors; its cylinder was replaced in 2005 and its detector edge in 2021. Two 100-gallon water heaters were permitted in 2001.

Permitted work since 2016: a Chapter 93 soft-story retrofit by Optimum Seismic with a Certificate of Compliance issued March 2, 2018; a 55-square Class A cool roof finaled October 5, 2017; a laundry room subpanel and GFCI outlets in January 2022; building-wide electrical subpanel replacement issued September 2022 and finaled in 2023; bathroom faucets in seven units and a new laundry sink in 2022; and engineered repair and reinforcement of the balconies in 20 units, finaled April 17, 2024.

Photographs of turned units show white cabinetry, granite counters, stainless appliances in several kitchens, plank flooring, wall air conditioners and sliding doors to private balconies. The building's rental advertisements describe intercom entry, the elevator, on-site management and parking, with the owner paying water, trash and the gardener.

What is not yet documented is the condition of every unit interior, the supply and drain piping, the heating and the parking count beyond the carport. None of it is unusual for a 1962 building, and a walk before launch lets the package answer those questions rather than leave them to a buyer's inspection. Two 2008 electrical permits, for bathroom exhaust fans and one smoke detector, expired without a final and are worth closing out before marketing.
market_narrative: Five closed sales of rent-stabilized buildings of 16 or more units, built between 1950 and 1969, recorded within 1.3 miles of the subject between May 2025 and August 2026. They closed at $4.9M to $12.6M, $269,750 to $350,000 per unit and $288 to $356 per SF, with medians of $300,000 per unit and $343 per SF. The closest match, 725 N Sweetzer Ave, a 21-unit 1965 elevator building north of Melrose, recorded at $6.3M in June 2026. The nearest, 6300 Orange St on the same street, recorded at $4.9M in May 2025 after 66 days on the market at 98% of its asking price.

Every one of those buyers borrowed against cheaper money than a buyer does today. Thirty days before each sale the 3-year Treasury stood between 3.58% and 4.23% and the 5-year between 3.72% and 4.31%; on September 16, 2026 they were 4.82% and 4.86% (U.S. Treasury constant maturity, via FRED). The gap runs from 0.59 points on the two August 2026 Shenandoah sales to 1.24 points on 6300 Orange.

The comps with a public listing history tell one story. 725 N Sweetzer listed at $7,995,000, fell out of escrow, expired and closed at 79% of that price; 142 S Wetherly closed at 83% of its $15,250,000 ask. The one priced near its value, 6300 Orange, sold in 66 days at 98% of its ask.
positioning_narrative: The right buyer values what is uncommon at this size: an elevator building in Beverly Grove with its seismic, balcony, roof and electrical work finished and documented, a Walk Score of 95, and occupied one-bedroom rents about 13% under the pro forma's $2,495 that move to market as tenants turn over. That buyer should be qualified early on two questions, whether they accept the underwritten insurance and repair figures or underwrite to the 2025 return, and whether they are financing at today's rates or buying with modest debt, because both decide where inside the range an offer lands.
rent_narrative: Rent evidence is read plan by plan in City of Los Angeles RSO buildings within 0.61 mile. Five one-bedroom asks in four buildings built from 1954 to 1975 run $2,287 to $2,495: $2,295 at the 1965 Sherholt on Holt Avenue, $2,287 and $2,395 at the 1969 elevator building at 1025 S Holt, $2,325 at Bloom on Olympic with a month free, and $2,495 for a fully remodeled unit at 423 S Sherbourne. With the building's own one-bedroom asks of $2,350 (unit 203, September 2026) and $2,385 (unit 207, October 2025), the median is $2,350. Two-bedroom asks run $2,799 to $3,300 on plans of 859 to 1,200 SF, with a median of $2,895.

The asking evidence centers on $2,350 for a turned one-bedroom and about $2,900 for a two-bedroom. The comparable two-bedrooms are larger, 1,000 to 1,200 SF against portal records of 825 to 900 SF for the subject's, which argues lower; the subject's elevator, balconies and updated kitchens argue higher. The pro forma carries $2,495 per one-bedroom, the top of the one-bedroom range and unit 103's current rent, and an average of $2,912 per two-bedroom, which puts the building at $658,740 of scheduled rent, 26.9% above the current $519,099 that carries units 201 and 301 at no rent. The renovated ceiling, 8534 Colgate with in-unit laundry at $3,595, is a different product and is not carried.
valuation_narrative: The recommended list price is $5.75M, the top of an opinion of value of $5.5M to $5.75M. At $5.75M the building prices at $273,810 per unit and $276.87 per SF. Current scheduled rent of $519,099, which carries the manager's unit and unit 301 at no rent, less a 3% vacancy reserve plus $4,200 of laundry, gives $507,726 of effective gross income; operating expenses of $211,092, with taxes reassessed at 1.20% of the list price, the owner's own $27,390 of utilities and the required on-site manager, leave net operating income of $296,634, a 5.16% cap rate and an 11.08 GRM. At the pro forma's $658,740 of scheduled rent the net operating income is $426,668 and the cap rate 7.42%. With 50% down and a $2.875M loan at 6.50% amortized over 30 years, the illustration in the model, debt coverage is 1.36 and the first-year cash-on-cash return 2.73%.

This price is set by yield. At the list the cap rate is 5.16%, above the 4.74% that 6300 Orange shows on its own statement with its taxes restated at its sale price, and the subject is the better building: newer, served by an elevator, with larger units and the mandated work done. The 11.08 GRM runs above that building's 9.95 because current rent carries two of the 21 units at no rent; on the pro forma rents it is 8.73. On price per unit, $273,810 sits 10.3% below the $305,382 average of the five sales and 8.7% under 725 N Sweetzer, the same-size 1965 elevator building at $300,000, and just above 6300 Orange at $272,222 and 1534 S Shenandoah at $269,750. On price per SF, $276.87 sits below all five sales, which run $288 to $356.

The discount to the comps comes from the cost of money: every one of them financed into Treasury yields 0.59 to 1.24 points lower than today's. A buyer borrowing at today's rates pays less for the same income, so this opinion sits at a 5.16% cap and does not ask a buyer to pay the comps' prices at today's cost of money. Pricing the building where a financed buyer's numbers work from the first day avoids the gap between ask and sale that cost 725 N Sweetzer and 142 S Wetherly months on the market.

Buying with modest debt makes today's Treasury level less of an obstacle for this buyer than for a fully financed one.

rent_control.conclusion: Registered with the Los Angeles Housing Department under the City's Rent Stabilization Ordinance for all 21 units (certificate of occupancy issued 09/20/1962, before the October 1978 cutoff). In-place rents rise only by the annual RSO allowance; a unit resets to market when a tenant leaves voluntarily under Costa-Hawkins. The building is covered by the City's just-cause protections and has no Ellis Act history.

zoning.conclusion: R3-1-O (Medium Residential) in the Wilshire community plan, Council District 5, on a 13,479 SF interior lot. The parcel sits in a liquefaction zone and a methane zone. The property is presented as built: a 21-unit, three-story building with an attached carport, and no further entitlement is relied upon.

development.conclusion: No development scenario is relied upon in this valuation. The parcel is Transit Oriented Communities Tier 3, within a half mile of a major transit stop and listed as a Housing Element site; redevelopment of an occupied RSO building would carry replacement, relocation and Ellis Act obligations, so these are noted for context only.
